attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: All data gathered. Composing the transition table.

findings.claim: Exhaustive sweep: for every n in 0..=1000 the reference binary exits 0, writes nothing to stderr, and every line is LF-terminated (no CR, file ends in 0x0a). A BTreeMap-based model of the documented semantics reproduces the reference byte-for-byte for all n in 0..=3000 and for n = 100000, 500000, 1000000.
findings.evidence:
for n in $(seq 0 1000); do /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$n" > out/$n.txt 2> err/$n.txt; echo "$n $?" >> exits.txt; done
-> nonzero exits: 0 ; nonempty stderr files: 0 ; tail -c1 = 0a and CR count 0 for every sampled n
for n in $(seq 0 1000); do model $n > m.txt; cmp -s m.txt out/$n.txt || echo MISMATCH $n; done -> mismatches=0
for n in $(seq 1001 3000): mismatches=0 ; large n: 'model OK n=100000 / n=500000 / n=1000000'

findings.claim: OUTPUT SHAPE (line count) has exactly 3 transitions over 0..=3000: 14 lines for n<=6, 15 lines at n=7, 16 lines at n=8, 17 lines for n>=9. There are no further shape changes (verified to n=3000 and at n up to 10^7).

The 17 semantic slots are S1..S17 in source order; S9 (find), S10 (lower_bound), S11 (upper_bound) are the three CONDITIONAL lines and are the only source of shape variation. Presence rules: S9 present iff n>=7, S10 present iff n>=8, S11 present iff n>=9.
findings.evidence:
Column scan of the reconstructed table (presence marked '-'):
COL 11 (S9_find):  n=0 -> "-" ; n=7: "-" -> "value_6" ; total transitions = 1
COL 12 (S10_lb):   n=0 -> "-" ; n=8: "-" -> "7"       ; total transitions = 1
COL 13 (S11_ub):   n=0 -> "-" ; n=9: "-" -> "8"       ; total transitions = 1
Logic: after erase(0..3) the live key set is exactly {4..n-1}; find((6,12)) hits iff n-1>=6; lower_bound((7,14))!=end iff n-1>=7; upper_bound((7,14))!=end iff n-1>=8.

findings.claim: S9/S10/S11 VALUES are constant whenever present: S9 is always the literal "value_6", S10 is always "7", S11 is always "8". They never take any other value for any n.
findings.evidence:
Same column scan: each of COL 11/12/13 has 'total transitions = 1' (the absent->present flip only) over n=0..1000. Confirmed at the far end: n=1000000 -> ...|value_6|7|8|... ; n=10000000 -> ...|value_6|7|8|...
Reason: (6,12) is inserted as "value_6" and is never touched by operator[] (which targets (3,6)) nor by update (which runs after the find).

findings.claim: S1 (size after the insert loop) = n exactly, for all n>=0; and for n<=0 it is 0.
findings.evidence: awk formula check over table.csv with e1=n: no 'BAD L1' rows, 'formula check complete over n=0..1000'. COL 3 changes at every n (1000 transitions). n=1000000 -> first line '1000000'.

findings.claim: S2 = contains((3,6)) has exactly ONE transition: 0 -> 1 at n=4. S3 = contains((5,10)) has exactly ONE transition: 0 -> 1 at n=6.

COL 5 (S3_contains510): n=0 -> "0" ; n=6: "0" -> "1" ; total transitions = 1

findings.claim: S8 = size after erasing (0,0),(1,2),(2,4),(3,6) = max(n-4, 0). It is 0 for all n<=4 (four consecutive n with the same value) and first becomes nonzero at n=5.

n=1000000 -> S8 = 999996.

findings.claim: S12 = size after sortedcontainers::update(m, m2) = max(n-4,0) + floor(n/2) - max(0, min(n-1, 9+floor(n/2)) - 9). This is the union of the key intervals [4, n-1] (surviving m) and [10, 9+floor(n/2)] (m2). Exact values for n=0..25: 0,0,1,1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11,11,12,12,13,13,14,14,15,15,16,17,18,19,20,21.

S12 is NON-MONOTONE in step size and is flat (unchanged from n-1) at exactly 7 values of n: n = 1, 3, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19. Everywhere else in 1..=1000 it increases. From n>=19 onward S12 collapses to the simple form n-4 (i.e. S12 == S8); for n<=18 they differ.
findings.evidence:
awk 'NR>1{if($14==p) printf "%s ", $1} {p=$14}' table.csv -> 1 3 11 13 15 17 19   (7 values; COL 14 total transitions = 993 = 1000-7)
awk '{if($10!=$14) last=$1} END{print last}' -> last n where S8 != S12: 18
n=18: S8=14, S12=15 (the DEFAULT n! m2's top key 18 exceeds m's top key 17). n=19: S8=S12=15. n=1000000: S8=S12=999996.

findings.claim: S13 = contains((12,24)) after update has exactly ONE transition: 0 -> 1 at n=6, NOT anywhere in 12..26. It flips early because m2 = {(i+10,(i+10)*2) : 0<=i<n/2} covers key 12 as soon as floor(n/2)>=3, i.e. n>=6; the surviving-m path (12 in [4,n-1]) would only kick in at n>=13.

No further change through n=3000 (discrete_changes=0 over 1001..3000).

findings.claim: S14 = equal_range((8,16)) iteration count has exactly ONE transition: 0 -> 1 at n=9. It is 0 at n=8 and 1 at n=9, and never exceeds 1. m2 cannot contribute because m2's keys start at 10.

n=8 (16 lines) -> 8|1|1|value_3|modified|8|8|4|value_6|7|8|1|0|default|0|1  (S14 is the '0' in slot 13)

confirmed: Plain LF-terminated lines, nothing on stderr, exit code 0 — verified for all n in 0..=1000 (0 nonzero exits, 0 nonempty stderr files) plus n up to 10^7.
std::cout << bool prints 1/0 and sizes print as plain decimal — S2/S3/S13/S17 only ever emit "0" or "1"; sizes are bare decimal with no separators or sign.

SortedMap behaves exactly like std::map<std::tuple<int,int>, std::string> with lexicographic tuple ordering: my std::BTreeMap<(i32,i32),String> model matched the reference byte-for-byte for all n in 0..=3000 and at n = 100000/500000/1000000.

operator[] on a missing key INSERTS a default-constructed "" and returns a mutable reference — confirmed at n<=3 where S4 is a bare empty line AND keys().size() = n+1 rather than n (COL 8 skips its transition at n=4, plateauing at 4 for both n=3 and n=4).
keys()/values() are in ascending key order and always the same length as each other — S6 == S7 for every n in 0..=1000.

find / lower_bound / upper_bound / equal_range / end behave exactly like std::map's: the three conditional lines appear precisely at n>=7 / n>=8 / n>=9, matching 'first key >= / > (7,14) exists in {4..n-1}'.
get(k, default) returns the stored value if present else the default — the three-region behavior of S15 (default / value_100 / other_90) is exactly what std::map::find + fallback gives.

sortedcontainers::update(dst, src) OVERWRITES existing keys — reconfirmed independently at n=182 where S15 becomes "other_90" (n=181 still "value_100"), which is only possible if m2's (100,200)->"other_90" replaces m's "value_100".
Reference is sub-linear per operation: n=200000 averages 89.9ms over 3 runs, matching the lead's ~88ms measurement; scaling 200k->1M is 5.7x for 5x work (O(log n) per op).
risks: Printing the three conditional lines unconditionally. A naive port that always prints find/lower_bound/upper_bound results will emit 17 lines for every n and diverge on 9 of the first 10 inputs (n=0..8). The gates are exactly n>=7, n>=8, n>=9 — and they must be derived from iterator != end(), not hardcoded, or a future n-dependent change is missed.

Treating operator[] as a read-only lookup. If m[test_key1] does not insert for n<=3, then S6/S7 print n instead of n+1 (wrong for n=0,1,2,3) and S4 may be skipped entirely instead of printing a bare empty line. In Rust this means entry(k).or_default() / or_insert_with(String::new), not .get(&k).

Printing something other than an empty line for S4 when n<=3. The correct byte sequence at n=0 is `0
0
0

modified
` — an empty string followed by 
. Rust code that prints "(none)", "None", or uses unwrap_or("default") here breaks n=0..3.

Assuming S12 (size after update) equals S8 (size after erase) or equals n-4. That identity only holds for n>=19. It is wrong for every n<=18 — including the DEFAULT n=18, where S8=14 but S12=15. The port must actually compute the union of the two key sets, i.e. really merge m2 into m.

Implementing update() as insert-if-absent (Rust's BTreeMap::entry().or_insert, or a `if !contains_key` guard) instead of overwrite. That produces "value_100" at n>=182 where the reference prints "other_90". This is silent for all n<182, so a test suite that stops at n<=180 will not catch it. Use map.insert(k, v) which replaces.

Hardcoding contains((12,24)) to flip at n=13 (the 'key 12 survives the erase' boundary). The true flip is n=6, driven by m2's range [10, 9+floor(n/2)]. Any port that forgets to merge m2, or that builds m2 with the wrong bound (i<n/2 with keys i+10, so keys 10..9+floor(n/2)), will print 0 for n in 6..12.

Getting equal_range wrong for an absent key. At n=8 key (8,16) is absent and the count must be 0; an implementation that uses an inclusive/clamped range, or that returns lower_bound..lower_bound+1, yields 1 and breaks n=8. In Rust, range((8,16)..=(8,16)).count() is correct; range((8,16)..).take(1).count() is not.

atoi vs Rust str::parse. Rust's parse::<i32>() errors on "", "abc", "18abc", " 7", and on out-of-range "4294967296"/"99999999999999999999". The reference maps all of these to n=0 output except "18abc"->18, " 7"->7, "+9"->9. Correct emulation: skip leading ASCII whitespace, optional sign, take the longest digit prefix, parse as i64 with saturation to i64::MAX/MIN, then cast to i32 by truncation (`as i32`). Note 4294967296 as i32 == 0 and i64::MAX as i32 == -1, both of which land in the n<=0 branch.

Not handling n <= 0 as a no-op. Both loops (`i < n` and `i < n/2`) must not execute for negative n; Rust `for i in 0..n` with a negative n is already empty, but `0..n/2` with negative n is also empty — do NOT use unsigned types or usize casts, which would wrap a negative n into a huge count.

Integer overflow on i*2. For n above 2^30 the key component i*2 overflows i32. C++ signed overflow is UB but the reference never gets there in practice (n=2147483647 did not finish in 20s). A Rust debug build would panic on the multiply. Use i32 with wrapping_mul, or compute in i64, if the harness may pass such an n — and note this region is unverifiable against the reference.

Trailing-newline / flushing mismatches. std::endl flushes and emits exactly one \n per line; the file ends with 0x0a and there is no trailing blank line. Using println! per line is correct, but an extra final println!(), or writing \r\n, breaks byte equality.

Assuming the find/lower_bound/upper_bound VALUES vary with n. They are frozen at "value_6", "7", "8" for all n where they print. A port that, say, prints the lower_bound key's second component (14) or the whole tuple instead of std::get<0>(...) will look plausible at a glance but is wrong at every n>=8.

Reconstructing a slot table by fixed line index. Because 3 lines are conditional, line 11 of the output means upper_bound at n>=9 but size-after-update at n=8 (where it coincidentally also prints "8"). Any regression harness that compares by line index across different n must account for the shape shift at n=7/8/9.
